articles.title: U.S. infant bleeding episodes jump as vitamin K refusals rise, two studies find
articles.summary: Rates of life-threatening bleeding in U.S. infants have risen sharply since 2017 as parents increasingly refuse ​protective newborn doses of vitamin K, two studies found.
articles.body: CHICAGO, Nov 5 — Rates of life-threatening bleeding in U.S. infants have risen sharply since 2017 as parents increasingly refuse ​protective newborn doses of vitamin K, a trend that coincides with a growing wave of mistrust toward vaccines and other newborn interventions, two studies published on Thursday ‌found. The studies are the first to show that bleeding rates in U.S. infants have increased along with rising refusals of vitamin K shots. Babies are not born with enough vitamin K, an essential nutrient that helps blood clot, and vitamin K injections at birth have been standard for over 60 years. As a result, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention does not track rates of vitamin K refusals or bleeding. Vitamin K refusals have been rising steadily ​since the covid-19 pandemic, but have accelerated under Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who spent decades sowing mistrust about vaccines before taking the nation’s top health post. He has ​since dropped childhood recommendations for six vaccines. Changes to the childhood vaccination schedule are on hold over a legal challenge. Health experts say the mixed ⁠messages have raised doubts among many parents about routine newborn treatments, including vitamin K. A Department of Health and Human Services spokesperson said the CDC still recommends vitamin K shots for newborns but ​declined to say whether the agency would begin tracking rates of vitamin K refusals or bleeding events. A study published in JAMA last December by Dr. Kristan Scott and colleagues at the Children’s Hospital ​of Philadelphia showed that more than 5% of U.S. babies did not receive a vitamin K shot in 2024, a 77% increase since 2017. The latest data, published in JAMA and JAMA Pediatrics, show rates of vitamin K refusals have continued to climb, and begin to connect the dots between rising refusals of the essential vitamin and increased bleeding episodes. While these studies do not prove causation, the fact that the rates of bleeding have increased so dramatically ​at the same time vitamin K refusals and deficiencies have risen is significant, said Dr. Steven Woolf, an epidemiologist at Virginia Commonwealth University, whose study appeared in JAMA Pediatrics. Providing vitamin K shots ​at birth has been the standard of care since 1961. “Now we’re stepping away from that and we’re seeing the consequences,” he said. Woolf and colleagues studied medical records from 11 million infants six months and younger between 2017 ‌and 2025. ⁠During that time, the percentage of newborns who received a vitamin K shot fell from 97.7% to 95%, while the rate of vitamin K deficiency bleeding nearly quadrupled and appeared to be accelerating. Of more than 11 million births, there were a total of 5,217 bleeding events over that multi-year period. “The rate in 2025 was approximately double what it was in 2024,” Woolf said. The team noted that the peak in 2025 coincides with eroding trust in public health following the COVID pandemic, rising vaccine hesitancy and growing parental skepticism around newborn interventions. An exclusive analysis for Reuters of more than 1 million births nationwide ​by health data and analytics company Truveta found ​the percentage of vitamin K refusals accelerated ⁠sharply in the first half of 2026, jumping by more than 57% from January through June. In Scott’s new study, published in JAMA, the team analyzed medical records on more than 5.2 million US infants born between 2017 and 2025. During that time, the rate of newborns who did not receive a ​vitamin K shot more than doubled to 6.8% in 2025 from 3.1% in 2017. It also jumped from the 5.1% refusal rate at ​the end of 2024. Babies who ⁠did not receive a vitamin K shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding within the first 6 months of life compared with babies who did. They also had more than twice the risk of bleeding in the brain in their first six months, and death with a bleeding diagnosis during their hospital stay after birth. The authors calculated that for every 114 newborns who do not receive a vitamin K shot ⁠at birth, one ​additional bleeding event would occur. In June, Representative Kim Schrier of Washington and Senator Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, both Democrats, ​called on the CDC to start tracking these bleeding events. Dr. Elizabeth Wolf, a pediatrician at Children’s Hospital of Richmond, who led the VCU study, said the findings call for clear messages from all levels of public health about the need ​for vitamin K. “Similar to the recent measles outbreaks, we are seeing the real-world implications of growing mistrust of doctors and public health professionals,” she said.

articles.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to higher stroke risk, study finds
articles.summary: A study of nearly 450,000 adults found that both casual and heavy marijuana users faced higher odds of stroke and cardiovascular disease than non-users.
articles.body: A new study of nearly 450,000 American adults links cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease. The findings, scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9, show that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users. Researchers analyzed survey responses collected between 2020 and 2024 through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System. SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA People who reported using cannabis between one and five days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease than non-users. Those using it 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds. "This study raises important concerns about cannabis use and cardiovascular health, particularly stroke," Dr. Kristen "Nicke" Worth, an Ohio-based physician and medical adviser at NuggMD, a telehealth platform for medical marijuana evaluations, told Fox News Digital. "One finding I found particularly interesting was that people who used cannabis just one to five days per month had somewhat higher reported odds of a previous stroke than people who used it more frequently," added Worth, who was not involved in the study. Low-frequency users had 40% higher odds of a reported stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds. The study found no statistically significant link between cannabis use and heart attacks. MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS "That isn't what we'd necessarily expect from a straightforward dose-response relationship, where greater exposure is associated with greater risk. But we shouldn't interpret this as evidence that heavier use is safer," Worth said. The method of consumption did not change the outcome. Whether participants smoked, vaped or consumed edibles like gummies, the risk remained consistent, according to the researchers. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ "We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward," said lead author Dr. Aabha Divya, an assistant professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Tulane University School of Medicine, in an AHA press release. "We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease." The study comes amid growing commercial availability and use of the drug across the country. According to the research team, about one in six adults reported past-month cannabis use in 2024, up from one in 10 in 2020 — a 51% increase over four years. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER Dr. Robert L. Page II, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of Colorado and an American Heart Association volunteer expert who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge common assumptions about the drug's safety. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES "In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case," Page said in a press release. "Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events." "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report." Page added that doctors should question patients about marijuana use just as they do with cigarettes and alcohol. Researchers noted several key limitations to the findings. Because the study was observational and captured data from only a single point in time, it can only show a statistical link and cannot prove that cannabis causes heart disease or strokes. The data also relied on telephone surveys, leaving room for errors in participants' memory regarding their medical diagnoses and drug use. Additionally, the researchers did not track product strength, THC potency or total amounts consumed. The findings remain preliminary until vetted through the full, peer-reviewed publication process. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "For patients, I wouldn't recommend making abrupt treatment decisions based on one preliminary study, but I wouldn't dismiss these findings," Worth said. "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report." "Anyone using cannabis, medically or recreationally, should discuss their cardiovascular history, existing risk factors, medications and treatment alternatives with their healthcare professional," she added.

articles.title: The 1 Ingredient This GI Doc Adds to Her Coffee Every Morning To Boost Fiber Intake
articles.summary: In TODAY.com’s Expert Tip of the Day, a gastroenterologist reveals which supplement she recommends to people who struggle to get enough fiber in their diet.
articles.body: If you’re looking to improve your gut health, eating a diverse range of fiber-rich foods is your best bet. Most adults should aim to get about 25–38 grams of dietary fiber every day. However, it’s not easy for everyone to increase their intake or meet their fiber needs through diet alone. If you consistently struggle to eat enough fiber-rich foods or can’t meet the recommended daily fiber intake, you may benefit from taking a supplement, Dr. Trisha Pasricha, gastroenterologist and director of the Institute for Gut-Brain Research at Beth Israel Deaconness, tells TODAY.com. Although Pasricha always recommends a food-first strategy to patients, fiber supplements can help fill in the gaps. There are plenty of pills, powders and gummies to choose from — which one is best? Here’s the only fiber supplement Pasricha recommends: Gut Health Tip of the Day: Try Psyllium Husk Supplements If You Don’t Enough Fiber “I usually never recommend supplements because the data is so weak, but this is one where it’s strong,” Pasricha says. Psyllium husks are a plant-based fiber supplement that add bulk to stool and help move it out of the body, per Cleveland Clinic. “Psyllium is the fiber queen,” says Pasricha. Why It Matters Psyllium husks are predominantly soluble fiber, which absorbs water and becomes a gel-like substance in the gastrointestinal tract. In addition to bulking and softening stool, this type of fiber helps slow down digestion, stabilizes blood sugar and promotes bowel regularity, Pasricha explains. Psyllium husk also helps lower cholesterol by binding to bile, which reduces the amount of cholesterol the body absorbs, she adds. How to Get Started It’s a good idea to consult your doctor or pharmacist before starting a new supplement, especially if you are pregnant or have any underlying conditions. When taking psyllium husk, always follow the directions on the supplement labeling. The golden rule is to start low and slow, says Pasricha. Increasing your fiber intake too quickly can cause digestive upset. It’s also very important to drink plenty of water when taking psyllium, says Pasricha. Aim to consume at least one full glass (240 milliliters) with your supplement, per the Cleveland Clinic. You can also mix the psyllium husk into other drinks or food. “I mix it in my coffee every morning,” Pasricha says. Another one of Pasricha’s favorite hacks is to stir the powder into pumpkin overnight oats, which provide additional fiber. TODAY’s Expert Tip of the Day series is all about simple strategies to make life a little easier. Every Monday through Friday, different qualified experts share their best advice on diet, fitness, heart health, mental wellness and more.

articles.title: Sugar-free sweets: Healthy choice or clever label?
articles.summary: Walk into any Mumbai mithai shop and you may find a counter labelled \"sugar‑free.\" For a person living with diabetes sugar‑free can look like a guilt‑free
articles.body: Walk into any Mumbai mithai shop and you may find a counter labelled "sugar‑free." For a person living with diabetes sugar‑free can look like a guilt‑free invitation. Does sugar‑free automatically mean diabetes‑friendly? Sugar‑free does not always mean diabetes‑friendly.“Sugar‑free" describes sugar content; "sugar‑free" does not mean carbohydrate‑free, calorie‑free or healthy. Many sugar‑free mithais, chocolates, biscuits and desserts still contain flour, starch, milk solids, ghee, cream or considerable saturated fat. These ingredients can raise blood glucose add calories and make weight management more difficult.Sweetness may come from sweeteners such as stevia, sucralose or aspartame. Sugar‑free sweets usually have direct effect on blood glucose when consumed within approved limits. Other sugar‑free sweets contain sugar alcohols, called polyols, including maltitol, sorbitol, xylitol and erythritol.Polyols generally cause a glucose rise than ordinary sugar but "smaller" does not mean "zero." Maltitol, commonly used in sugar‑free chocolate can still produce a glucose response. Larger amounts of polyols may also cause gas, bloating, abdominal discomfort or diarrhoea.The American Diabetes Association’s 2026 Standards of Care states that non‑nutritive sweeteners may replace sugar‑sweetened products in moderation and for the term provided the substitution actually reduces total carbohydrate and calorie intake. Sugar‑free sweets are tools but sugar‑free sweets do not convert sweets into health foods.Before buying ignore the promise, on the front and study the nutrition panel on the back. Check serving size, total carbohydrate, calories, saturated fat and the ingredient list. Compare sugar‑free sweets values with the version. Remember that a small stated serving can make almost any product appear harmless.People using mealtime insulin may require guidance because different polyols are absorbed differently. Sugar‑free sweets must never be used to treat hypoglycaemia; absorbed glucose is required.An occasional small portion of sugar‑free sweets can fit into a diabetes plan. For snacking whole fruit, nuts, seeds or unsweetened curd usually provide better nutrition and greater fullness.Sugar‑free is a label, not a licence. Read the carbs respect the portion.Removing sugar does not remove consequences; the whole sweet still counts for glucose, weight and long‑term heart health too.Dr Altamash Shaikh, Consultant Endocrinologist, Saifee Hospital, MumbaiGet the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: Missing 13-year-old girl found dead at Raiganj forest, family alleges ‘rape’
articles.summary: Decomposed body of missing 13-year-old girl found in Kulik forest, Raiganj; family alleges sexual assault. Police probe underway, post-mortem awaited.
articles.body: Malda: A decomposed body of a 13-year-old girl, who had been missing since Tuesday, was recovered from Kulik forest in Raiganj, North Dinajpur on Thursday. The girl’s family alleged she was sexually assaulted before being murdered, as her clothes were found torn. Police, however said the investigation was underway and that they were awaiting the post-mortem report to ascertain the circumstances of her death.The girl, who had reportedly dropped out of school two years ago, had left her home in Bogram, under Raiganj police station on a bicycle on Tuesday afternoon to collect clothes from a self-help group worker. When she failed to return by evening, her family began looking for her among relatives and acquaintances. After their search yielded no results, they lodged a missing person’s diary at the local police station that night.On Thursday afternoon, some locals passing through Kulik forest, around 3km from Raiganj town, noticed a foul smell emanating from the woods. On searching the area, they spotted the decomposed body and alerted the police. The family was subsequently called to identify the remains and confirmed that it was the missing girl. The victim’s father alleged that she had been raped before being killed, citing the condition of her clothes and body.Police recovered the body and sent it to Raiganj Medical College and Hospital, where a post-mortem examination was conducted on Thursday night in the presence of a magistrate.An investigation has been launched, with six teams deployed to probe the case. Police are examining CCTV footage from Kulik forest and adjoining areas, while a dog squad has also been pressed into service. Investigators are additionally focusing on the Abdul Ghata Bandh area, where the girl was last traced. articles.title: Armed men kill at least 33 in village in Ebola-hit eastern DRC
articles.summary: Locals blame ADF armed group, which pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, for the deadly raids on North Kivu villages.
articles.body:
Armed men thought to be linked to an ISIL (ISIS)-affiliated group have raided villages in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), killing dozens of people, according to authorities and civil society groups.

The attackers also set fire to a ⁠health post during their overnight assault on Cantine, about 50km west of Beni in North Kivu province, forcing ⁠patients with confirmed and suspected Ebola infections to flee.

Fighters with the Allied Democratic Forces (ADF) armed group set fire to several houses and killed civilians, Beni territorial administrator Colonel ⁠Charles Omeonga told the Reuters news agency on Friday.

Justin Paluku, head of a local civil society group, also blamed the ADF for the attack.

“So far, we have counted 33 bodies and more than 50 houses set on fire, along with various other forms of material destruction,” he told the AP news agency.

Tchetche Aliamini, another local ⁠civil society leader, confirmed the death toll to Reuters and said that most of the victims suffered gunshot wounds, while others had been burned or hacked with machetes.

The violence forced many villagers to flee to other parts of the province, where the fastest-spreading Ebola outbreak in history is raging.

Among those who fled were 180 patients from the local hospital, including suspected Ebola cases and one confirmed Ebola case, said Christian Kakule, medical director of the Kelekele Hospital Centre in Cantine.

“High-risk contacts and other individuals under monitoring have all fled,” he said. “Our concern is that when probable cases end up out in the open like this, they can become a source of transmission and trigger an outbreak of the disease.”

He said there was gunfire and homes were set ablaze as close as 50 metres from the hospital.

North Kivu currently ‌accounts for almost half of all new infections in the DRC’s Bundibugyo outbreak and is the second most affected province after the epicentre, Ituri.

North Kivu was the epicentre of three previous Ebola outbreaks, including one in 2018-2020, which until this year was the DRC’s largest and deadliest.

The Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has recorded more than 10,000 cases and 5,300 Ebola deaths ‌across ‌the DRC .

The ADF, which has roots in Uganda and pledged allegiance to ISIL in 2019, has long operated in the border region and routinely attacks civilians. In July 2025, it killed 66 people in eastern DRC in what the United Nations called a “bloodbath”.

About 100 other armed groups operate in the DRC, most prominently the Rwanda-backed M23 , which has seized key cities in the east of the country while Ebola cases increase.

“This represents a major security failure,” Paluku, of the civil society group, told AP. “Given the number of loyalist and security forces deployed in this area, it is incomprehensible how the enemy managed to bypass their defences to kill civilians and inflict such significant material and human casualties.”

articles.title: Alzheimer's warning signs could emerge years before memory loss, study finds
articles.summary: A Science Advances study reveals how brain scan connectivity patterns predict Alzheimer's disease years before memory loss or cognitive decline.
articles.body: Small changes in how parts of the brain communicate with one another can help predict a person’s likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease years before any memory lapses appear, according to a study published in Science Advances. Stanford Medicine researchers used brain scans and a computer model to look for early clues about why some older adults develop memory and thinking problems while others stay sharp. Investigators examined resting brain scans from two opposing groups: patients diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and older individuals known as "super agers," whose memory capabilities match people decades younger. SUBTLE CHANGE IN HOW YOU SPEAK COULD BE EARLY SIGN OF DEMENTIA RISK, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Instead of looking for physical hallmarks like amyloid plaque accumulation or brain shrinkage, the researchers studied how different parts of the brain communicate with one another. By comparing the two groups’ brain activity patterns, the researchers calculated a measurement called the Alzheimer’s resilience-vulnerability connectome score, or ARC score, that distinguishes super agers from people with Alzheimer’s with about 85% accuracy. "I'm excited we established a signature that can help us better understand the difference between people who can maintain excellent cognitive performance and people who show cognitive decline," Yu Zhang, the study's senior author and an assistant professor of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford Medicine, said in a press release. DEMENTIA RISK MAY BE LINKED TO SEEMINGLY HARMLESS DAILY HABIT, NEW RESEARCH SUGGESTS Next, the scientists applied the scoring model to more than 1,300 cognitively unimpaired adults aged 55 to 70. Although all the adults scored normally on memory tests, their brain scans showed differences: Some had activity patterns similar to super agers, while others had patterns more like those seen in people with Alzheimer’s. CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES Over follow-up periods of up to 12 years, with most participants tracked for five to six years, those whose brain activity more closely resembled Alzheimer’s patterns showed faster declines in memory and thinking, developed more amyloid plaques and were more likely to be diagnosed with the disease, the researchers found. The team found that the ARC score matched or outperformed standard risk measures, including amyloid and tau biomarkers as well as genetic testing, in spotting early decline. "We compared the ARC score with existing biomarkers in predicting people converting to Alzheimer's disease," lead author Kanhao Zhao, a postdoctoral scholar in psychiatry at Stanford Medicine, said in the release. And if we combine our score with the existing biomarkers, the prediction performance improves." A central challenge in treating the disease is that physical damage often begins decades before patients notice memory lapses, at which point treatments offer limited benefit. Researchers stressed that the brain scan method is not yet ready for doctors to use on its own to diagnose Alzheimer’s. More studies are needed to confirm its accuracy and compare it with other new tests. However, understanding how brain activity differs between healthy aging and neurodegeneration could help researchers test future treatments, including techniques that stimulate the brain without surgery. articles.title: Fitness influencer's vacation getaway takes scary turn after headache leads to ICU
articles.summary: Khiana Smith was rushed by ambulance to a Bali hospital after a severe headache and light sensitivity led to a meningitis diagnosis in the ICU.
articles.body: A 23-year-old fitness influencer's vacation took a frightening turn after she suddenly became seriously ill in Bali. Australian fitness coach Khiana Smith said in a TikTok video that she was hospitalized after developing a severe headache and sensitivity to light. She later revealed in another video that she had been diagnosed with meningitis. Smith said she knew something was wrong when she woke up with what she described as the "worst headache." DEADLY LEGIONNAIRES' DISEASE OUTBREAK SPARKS CONCERN IN MAJOR US CITY: KNOW THE SYMPTOMS "I couldn't even get out of bed," Smith said in the TikTok video. "It was so intense I couldn't even open my eyes properly. I was really sensitive to light. I couldn't stand up without falling over." She initially waited to see whether she would feel better, but said she woke up the following morning feeling "10 times worse." She was eventually taken to a hospital by ambulance, where testing revealed the infection. Dr. Alfred Joshua, a California-based board-certified emergency room physician and former chief medical officer, told Fox News Digital that Smith's reported symptoms included several warning signs that should be taken seriously. "She started having symptoms of severe headache, having difficulty with light," Joshua said. "And then she started having difficulty walking, and then eventually slurred speech." Symptoms can include headache, fever, stiff neck and sensitivity to light. Trouble walking or speaking, confusion and extreme tiredness are more serious signs that should prompt immediate medical attention, Joshua said. The seriousness of the illness can also depend on what is causing it. Joshua said viral meningitis often resolves on its own, while bacterial meningitis can progress rapidly and requires prompt treatment with antibiotics. Smith's condition later appeared to improve enough for her to leave the ICU, but she said she had to return after continuing to experience head pain, light sensitivity and slurred speech. She also reported memory loss, and said swelling in her brain was preventing her from flying home. When meningitis is suspected, Joshua said doctors can use blood tests, brain imaging and a lumbar puncture to determine whether the infection is bacterial, viral or caused by something else.
